description: We are researchers looking to challenge ourselves
summary:
Firefighters learn much of what they know about fire behaviour on the fireline itself. Reading how wind, slope and fuel will push a fire, and noticing a wind shift before it traps you, are skills that save lives, but they are hard to practise safely. Spark-Shield fills that gap: a browser-based simulator where trainees face realistic fires on real landscapes.

To make those fires realistic, we start with where they are likely to begin. The NASA–ISRO NISAR radar sees through clouds and smoke and measures how much water the soil holds. Combining two months of NISAR soil moisture with weather, fuel and terrain, we estimate where a fire is most likely to start each day. The trainee then steps into a 3D view of that real terrain and faces a fire driven by real wind, fuel and slope. Past fires, recorded by the VIIRS and MODIS thermal satellites, can be replayed too.

We started with Nova Scotia, where we live, to fit the challenge's timeframe. Because NISAR observes the whole planet, the same approach could build training scenarios wherever wildfires threaten crews.
details:
What does it do?

The simulator has two parts.

The Fire Atlas is a map of Canada with a timeline. Past days show fires that really happened between 2018 and 2026. Today and the next seven days show predicted fire starts over Nova Scotia. Clicking a fire opens a briefing card: fuel type, terrain, NISAR soil moisture and the weather. Next to the card is a 3.2 km map of the area, where the trainee chooses a starting position.

For the demo, "today" is set to 15 July 2026, because summer is when fires are most frequent, which gives the widest choice of scenarios. The model only uses NISAR data and fire records from before that date. For the following seven days, it uses the weather actually recorded on those days. In everyday use, a weather forecast would take its place.

The first-person simulator then rebuilds the area the trainee selected in 3D (WebGL), with 30 m relief, 100 m fuel cells, and the roads and buildings from OpenStreetMap. The trainee walks the terrain, and moves more slowly uphill and through dense fuel. Water is simplified for now: the trainee has a 750 L supply with a 20 m reach, refilled at the fire truck or a lake. In reality, a firefighter on foot uses a hose line fed by a fire truck or a backpack pump of about 20 L, so making the equipment realistic is part of our next steps. The rules teach the fireline's hard lessons:

  • Water only knocks down low-intensity flames, so it has no effect on the head of a running fire.
  • Radiant heat damages the trainee's health within about 15 m of the flames.
  • The wind shifts partway through the scenario.

A heads-up display shows the distance to the fire and when it is expected to arrive, the wind, the fuel, the remaining water and health. A debrief reports the closest approach to the fire, the area saved, the water used and the number of homes protected. A typical fire takes about three days to cross that area, so simulation speed can be set anywhere from real time (1 second in the simulator = 1 second in real life) up to 1 second = 10 minutes.

How does it work?

The two satellite systems each do the job they are best at.

1. Where fires could start (NISAR)

NISAR data. NISAR has observed Canada since October 2025. We read 4,230 NISAR scenes (2,109 GCOV backscatter and 2,121 SME2 soil-moisture products) directly from NASA's Alaska Satellite Facility website. We extracted only the pixels we needed, since a single GCOV file is about 4.6 GB. Values were averaged over small neighbourhoods (about 600 m) to reduce radar speckle. For any given day we used only acquisitions from before that day, so the model never "sees" the fire it is predicting.

What the model learns from. For each of 611 Canadian fire starts in 2026 with NISAR coverage, we took the location where the fire started and about ten nearby locations that did not burn. We then followed every location day by day through the fire season. The result is about 145,000 location-days, of which 611 are fire starts. Because every fire's locations are pooled on each calendar day, one model learns both when fires happen (weather changes from day to day) and where they happen (fuel, terrain and radar change from place to place).

Inputs (31 in total):

  • Weather (NASA POWER): Canadian Fire Weather Index components, temperature, humidity, wind, recent rain
  • Fuel (Canadian fuel map): forest type, share of conifer, water and non-fuel within 1 km
  • Terrain (Copernicus DEM): elevation, slope, aspect
  • Fire history (Canadian fire databases): nearby past human- and lightning-caused fires, recent burns
  • Radar (NISAR SME2): 60-day mean soil moisture

Model. As a baseline, we used a regularised logistic regression. With a single season of fires, more flexible models such as gradient-boosted trees did not rank fires any better in our tests, and logistic regression lets us explain each input's effect in plain terms. The two strongest effects are a coniferous neighbourhood (2.1× the odds) and high temperature (1.6×). Drier soil over the past two months also raises the odds, which is what the physics would predict. In the future we would like to test other explainable models, such as generalised additive models (GAMs) or explainable boosting machines. These can capture non-linear effects, for example risk rising sharply above a certain temperature, while still showing how each input affects the result.

Testing. Every result is measured on fires the model never saw during training (five-fold cross-validation, grouped by fire). Overall ranking skill (AUC) is 0.74. The most useful measure for the simulator is how many real fire starts fall in the 20% of locations the model ranks highest each day:

  • Random guess: 20.0%
  • Weather only: 29.5%
  • Plus fuel, terrain and fire history: 41.7%
  • Plus NISAR soil moisture (final model): 44.5%

From probability to playable fire starts. Fires are rare (about 1 in 240 location-days), so "accuracy" would be meaningless: always predicting "no fire" would score 99.6%. The simulator doesn't need a complete warning map, only a handful of credible fire starts each day, so we chose a strict cut-off (probability ≥ 0.024). In testing it flags under 1% of location-days, and fires start there about 7 times more often than average. The trade-off is that it keeps only the riskiest 5% of real fire starts, which suits training scenarios but would not suit an alert system. Each day we apply the model to all 5.2 million burnable 100 m cells of Nova Scotia. The scenarios are the local peaks above the cut-off, spaced at least 7.5 km apart and capped at 25 per day. The number follows the weather: 11 fire starts on 15 July 2026, and none on 19 July after rain.

2. How fires spread (thermal satellites)

NISAR revisits a location every few days, which is too slow to follow a fire that can double in a few hours. For spread we used fire detections from the VIIRS and MODIS thermal satellites, which pass several times a day. We rebuilt 2,930 Canadian fires (2018–2026) on a 100 m grid. In total this is 34 million cells, each with the time it started burning, drawn from 274,000 satellite passes. The median timing uncertainty is under one hour. Fires observed too sparsely to time reliably were excluded (912 of 3,842).

Between passes, we filled in arrival times using a spread model. In this model a fire's rate of spread depends on the fuel type, increases sharply when the fire runs with the wind, and depends on the slope. Its seven parameters were fitted with a genetic algorithm on 2018–2024 fires and tested on 2025 fires. Wind turned out to matter a lot. Slope did not, at 100 m resolution. Historical scenarios replay the recorded arrival times, and predicted scenarios use the calibrated spread model.

Why NISAR soil moisture, and not more radar?

We also tested NISAR backscatter (HH and HV polarisations), seasonal trends, and change since autumn 2025. Together these raised the AUC slightly, to 0.748. We left them out for two reasons:

  • NISAR only reached Nova Scotia in June 2026, so the autumn and winter history those features need does not exist there yet.
  • Backscatter varies from one satellite pass to the next (viewing angle, orbit direction), which produced stripes across the provincial map.

Soil moisture is a physical measurement that stays consistent across passes and is available everywhere, so it is the radar input that works in practice today.

Benefits

  • Safe, realistic practice: trainees learn how wind, slope and fuel drive a fire, and what a wind shift does, before they meet it on the fireline.
  • Real places and real risk: scenarios happen on the actual terrain where crews work, on fires that did happen or plausibly could this week.
  • Scenarios that change with the weather: on a warm, dry day there are many candidate fire starts. After rain there are none.
  • Accessible: it runs in a desktop browser, works offline and needs no special hardware. Several trainees can use it at once.

Intended impact

We want to put NISAR's view of the landscape in front of firefighters and emergency-management trainees, and turn it into a concrete lesson: this ground is dry, this is how a fire here would behave, and this is how fast it could reach you. Longer term, the same pipeline could support pre-season training for at-risk communities wherever NISAR flies.

Why Nova Scotia, and where else it could work

We chose Nova Scotia because it is where we live, and because the hackathon's time limit and the amount of data involved meant we had to pick one region. The method itself is not tied to Nova Scotia. NISAR covers the whole planet, and every other input has a global or regional equivalent:

  • NASA POWER weather and VIIRS/MODIS fire detections (NASA FIRMS) are global.
  • Copernicus elevation and OpenStreetMap cover the world.
  • Fuel maps exist in many fire-prone regions, for example LANDFIRE in the United States and national fuel maps in Europe and Australia.

The same pipeline could generate training scenarios for California, the Mediterranean or Australia.

The training sample, 611 fires from one season, is small because NISAR is new, not because fires are scarce. Each new fire season adds hundreds of examples with radar history, so the model will improve as NISAR's record grows.

Tools, languages and software

  • Data and modelling: Python (pandas, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, shapely, scikit-learn; PyTorch for spread-model experiments; pyosmium for OpenStreetMap).
  • Simulator: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Three.js (WebGL). There is no game engine and there are no 3D model files. Terrain, trees, houses, fire, smoke and water are all generated in code.
  • Data: NISAR L2 GCOV and L3 SME2 (NASA–ISRO, via ASF DAAC); NASA POWER; VIIRS/MODIS active fire, national fire databases and the fuel map (Natural Resources Canada); Copernicus DEM; OpenStreetMap.
  • Hosting: a small Python web server on a laptop. No specialised hardware is needed.
  • Licence: open source under MIT.

How is it creative?

  • NISAR used for training, not just mapping: instead of a change map, the radar observations become a scenario a person can step into.
  • Each sensor does what it does best: slow, cloud-penetrating radar describes the conditions before a fire, and fast thermal satellites describe the fire itself.
  • Past and future on one timeline: the same interface replays what happened and previews what could happen this week.

What factors did we consider?

  • Data gaps: NISAR has no acquisitions over our study fires between February and May 2026. We required every location to have at least one radar acquisition in the 60 days before each day, which removed 90 early-season fire starts but kept the comparison fair.
  • Interpretability over complexity: with one season of data, a simple model generalised as well as complex ones and can be explained to a non-specialist.
  • Meaningful measures: we judged the model by how many real fires fall in its top-ranked areas, not by accuracy, and set the cut-off for what the simulator needs: few, credible fire starts rather than catching every fire.
  • Firefighter realism: we modelled limited water, suppression that only works at low intensity, radiant heat, terrain-dependent movement and a wind shift.
  • Safety and scope: Spark-Shield is a training tool, not an operational forecast. The 7-day window is a hindcast that uses observed weather, and real use would require weather forecasts.

What's next

Improving how the fire spreads. Predicted fires currently grow according to a simple fuel–wind–slope model. It is calibrated on real fires, but it is still an approximation. The next step is to learn spread directly from the real fires we rebuilt from thermal-satellite detections. The training set is ready: about 4,000 sequences from 356 fires, each a 4.8 km patch showing a fire front advancing in 6-hour steps, with fuel, terrain, weather and NISAR layers. The model we chose is a ConvLSTM, a neural network that reads a sequence of maps and predicts the next one, which suits the spread of a fire front. Its first benchmark is a simple baseline that predicts every cell next to the burned area will ignite next (F1 = 0.22). The short timeframe of the challenge didn't leave time to train it. It is the most direct way to make the simulator's fires behave more like real ones, and so to make the training more realistic.

Richer training:

  • Make it multiplayer, so a whole crew can train together and coordinate on the same fire.
  • Add the real tools of wildfire fighting, such as fire trucks, hose lines, water bombers like the Canadair, helicopters and bulldozers for firebreaks, each with its real-life limits: tank size, refill time, flight turnaround and crew size.

Better predictions:

  • Add measures of human activity (road and building density), since about two-thirds of Nova Scotia fires are human-caused.
  • Bring in more NISAR features once a full year of acquisitions is available.
